Especially if that data is available as open access and exploitable by others for both valid scientific reasons but potentially also by those with other motives.<\/jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.31838\/jcr.07.12.207","title":["PROVENANCE AWARE AUDIT TRAIL FRAMEWORK FOR SAAS PROVIDERS EFFICIENCY ASSESSMENT IN CLOUD ENVIRONMENT"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2020,6,2]]},"container-title":["Journal of critical reviews"],"type":"journal-article"},{"DOI":"10.32388\/fnozr5","title":["Audit Trail"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2020,2,2]]},"container-title":["Definitions"],"type":"reference-entry"},{"DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.6532518","title":["Institutional AI Accountability Fabric (IAAF): System and Method for Authority-Linked Decision Provenance, Human Override Capture, and Replayable Audit Reconstruction"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>The Institutional AI Accountability Fabric (IAAF) introduces a governance-oriented framework for preserving, reviewing, and reconstructing AI-assisted decisions in institutional settings. As artificial intelligence becomes more deeply embedded in enterprise, regulatory, and operational workflows, organizations face increasing difficulty in explaining how decisions were generated, whether they aligned with policy and delegated authority, how human supervisors altered recommendations, and whether those decisions can later be reconstructed for audit or review. The IAAF framework addresses this gap by linking AI-supported decisions to policy context, authority structures, supervisory intervention, and replayable accountability records. This publication outlines the conceptual architecture, decision-governance logic, and potential institutional applications of IAAF across sectors including financial services, healthcare, cybersecurity, infrastructure, and public administration.<\/jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.4135\/9781412983907.n110","title":["Audit Trail"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2005]]},"container-title":["Dictionary of Statistics & Methodology"],"type":"reference-entry"},{"DOI":"10.4135\/9781412952644.n35","title":["Audit Trail"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2007]]},"container-title":["Encyclopedia of Measurement and Statistics"],"type":"reference-entry"},{"DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.6493442","title":["HDP: A Lightweight Cryptographic Protocol for Human Delegation Provenance in Agentic AI Systems"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>Agentic AI systems increasingly execute consequential actions on behalf of human principals, delegating tasks through multi-step chains of autonomous agents. No existing standard addresses a fundamental accountability gap: verifying that terminal actions in a delegation chain were genuinely authorized by a human principal, through what chain of delegation, and under what scope. This paper presents the Human Delegation Provenance (HDP) protocol, a lightweight token-based scheme that cryptographically captures and verifies human authorization context in multi-agent systems. An HDP token binds a human authorization event to a session, records each agent's delegation action as a signed hop in an append-only chain, and enables any participant to verify the full provenance record using only the issuer's Ed25519 public key and the current session identifier. Verification is fully offline, requiring no registry lookups or third-party trust anchors. We situate HDP within the existing landscape of delegation protocols, identify its distinct design point relative to OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange (RFC 8693), JSON Web Tokens (RFC 7519), UCAN, and the Intent Provenance Protocol (draft-haberkamp-ipp-00), and demonstrate that existing standards fail to address the multi-hop, append-only, human-provenance requirements of agentic systems. HDP has been published as an IETF Internet-Draft (draft-helixar-hdp-agentic-delegation-00) and a reference TypeScript SDK is publicly available.<\/jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.6730343","title":["Provenance as Substrate: A Cryptographic Identifier Framework for Music Rights and Royalty Infrastructure"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>The music industry's identifier infrastructure is failing under loads it was never designed for. The International Standard Recording Code (ISRC), the International Standard Musical Work Code (ISWC), and the identity codes that bind them were built as administrative artifacts, reconciled through fuzzy matching across collection societies that do not share schemas. The Mechanical Licensing Collective alone holds hundreds of millions of dollars in unmatched royalties, most of it unclaimed because identifiers do not align across registries. Generative artificial intelligence compounds the problem: new tracks enter distribution at over one hundred thousand a day, and the matching infrastructure cannot keep up. In an earlier paper I argued that detection-based responses to AI-generated music are structurally falsifiable and that cryptographic provenance offers the only verification model that is not. This paper extends that argument from authorship verification to identifier infrastructure. I propose that the same cryptographic primitive used to verify provenance can serve as the substrate for music identification itself: a self-issuing, collision-resistant, signed identifier that binds authorship and identification in a single operation. The result is not a replacement for ISRC or ISWC but a substrate beneath them, capable of resolving legacy identifiers as aliases while making future works identifiable at the moment of creation rather than at the moment of registration. This paper describes the architecture, the registry federation model, the backward-compatibility layer for legacy catalog, and the standards-body adoption path, and surfaces open implementation questions including signature scheme selection, key management, and ownership transfer.<\/jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.6402298","title":["Provenance Over Detection: A Cryptographic Framework for Human Authorship Verification in Music Distribution"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>The proliferation of AI-generated music has exposed a structural flaw in how digital streaming platforms govern content authenticity. Current platform responses rely primarily on output-based detection-identifying AI-generated audio after the fact using algorithmic classifiers. These tools are unreliable, slow to adapt, and generate false positives at rates that threaten legitimate artists. This paper argues that detection is the wrong frame entirely. The solution is provenance: cryptographic verification of human authorship embedded at the point of creation and carried through the distribution chain. Drawing on existing standards including C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity, 2025), recent advances in audio watermarking (Digimarc, 2025; Ono, 2026), and blockchain-based session verification (Pandey, Singh, et al., 2025), this paper proposes a music-specific provenance framework that addresses AI detection, royalty attribution, rights management, and licensing transparency within a single embedded metadata layer. The framework is designed for DAW-level implementation with distribution-chain readability, adding negligible file overhead while creating a permanent, tamper-evident record of an audio asset's origin, authorship, and modification history.<\/jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.5012274","title":["The SEC's Consolidated Audit Trail Data Technologies"],"type":"book-chapter"},{"DOI":"10.14293\/pr2199.004155.v1","title":["A Comparative Analysis of Cryptographic vs. Heuristic Session Anchors for AI Commit Provenance in Distributed Version Control Systems"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,7,26]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>The proliferation of AI-generated code in software development introduces a critical challenge for distributed version control systems (DVCS): establishing irrefutable provenance and behavioral commit integrity. While cryptographic signatures (e.g., GPG) provide robust authentication of a committer's identity, they fail to anchor the intent or context of a commit, particularly distinguishing between human-authored and AI-generated contributions. This paper presents a comparative analysis of two architectural paradigms for establishing \"session anchors\"\u2014tamper-evident metadata bindings that link a commit to the specific development environment and workflow that produced it. We contrast a Cryptographic Session Anchor (CSA) , which employs a hybrid key-signing scheme (e.g., using ephemeral session keys or hardware security modules) to sign a comprehensive commit manifest, against a Heuristic Session Anchor (HSA) , which generates a probabilistic fingerprint of the development session based on a composite of behavioral telemetry (e.g., IDE activity, keystroke dynamics, clipboard history, and AI tool invocation patterns). Our methodology evaluates both anchors against a matrix of security properties (non-repudiation, collision resistance), performance overhead, resilience to replay attacks, and, crucially, their efficacy in AI commit provenance. Through empirical analysis on a corpus of mixed human and AI-generated commits, we find that while the CSA offers superior cryptographic guarantees and non-repudiation, the HSA provides a more granular, contextual layer of evidence, effectively capturing the nuance of AI interaction that pure cryptography obscures. We further demonstrate that a hybrid, tiered approach\u2014using the CSA for definitive integrity and the HSA for forensic explainability\u2014significantly enhances the trustworthiness of the commit history. Our findings provide a foundational framework for next-generation DVCS protocols that not only secure who committed the code, but also how and with what assistance it was created, offering a path toward verifiable and auditable AI-assisted software engineering.<\/jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.1007\/978-3-319-77525-8_100043","title":["Business Process Audit Trail"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2019]]},"container-title":["Encyclopedia of Big Data Technologies"],"type":"book-chapter"},{"DOI":"10.1007\/978-3-211-89836-9_335","title":["data audit trail"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2009]]},"container-title":["Dictionary of Pharmaceutical Medicine"],"type":"book-chapter"},{"DOI":"10.26434\/chemrxiv.15001263\/v2","title":["QENEX LAB: A Self-Contained Quantum Chemistry Platform with Reproducible Self-Assessed Compliance and Cryptographic Provenance Bundles"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026,5,27]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>QENEX LAB is a sovereign, air-gapped scientific computing platform for quantum chemistry and drug discovery, deployed on a single-server configuration with no external cloud or hardware dependencies. The platform provides 12 user-callable computational methods through a unified Molecule.compute() API (Hartree\u2013Fock, MP2, CCSD, CCSD(T), UCCSD, EOM-CCSD, CASSCF, DFT\/LDA\/B3LYP, TDDFT, DLPNO-CCSD, DMC) backed by 32 method-implementation modules and 6 basis sets (STO-3G, 6-31G*, cc-pVDZ, cc-pVTZ, aug-cc-pVDZ, aug-cc-pVTZ). Hartree\u2013Fock energies agree with PySCF references to sub-nanohartree precision (drift < 1 \u00d7 10\u207b\u2079 Hartree) on 5 of 6 reference-validated (molecule, basis) tuples; the worst case is sub-millihartree (3.4 \u00d7 10\u207b\u2074 Hartree on H\u2082O \/ cc-pVDZ via the native Obara\u2013Saika engine).<\/jats:p>\n                <jats:p>Compliance posture is self-assessed against six published rubrics with full reproducibility: NASA TRL 6\/9, DoD MRL 7\/10, NASA NPR 7150.2D Rev D (40\/42 PASS, 2 honest WARN), FAIR Principles for Research Software (20\/20), ISO\/IEC 25010:2011 (18\/18), and WIPO PCT Rule 11 (8\/8) \u2014 total 111\/113. These are self-assessments, not external audits by NASA, DoD, ISO, IEC, or WIPO. The platform ships with a cryptographic provenance system: every computed energy emits a runnable .qlang verification program plus an atoms.json geometry sidecar that an external auditor can re-execute.<\/jats:p>\n                <jats:p>The v2 preprint supersedes v1 (10.26434\/chemrxiv.15001263\/v1, March 2026); \u00a7V reconciles every v1 numeric claim against today's reproducer output and documents downward revisions where v1 was overstated. The companion open-source verifier subset (Apache 2.0, https:\/\/github.com\/qenex-ai\/qenex-verifier, Zenodo DOI 10.5281\/zenodo.20083483) lets any reviewer independently reproduce every numeric claim in this abstract on a clean machine.<\/jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.2139\/ssrn.7087439","title":["ConsentBus: Atomic Cross-SDK Privacy Consent Propagation with Cryptographic Audit for Mobile Applications"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2026]]},"type":"posted-content","abstract":"<jats:p>Modern mobile applications embed five to twenty or more third-party software development kits (SDKs)-analytics, advertising, attribution, and crash-reporting-each exposing a different proprietary consent management API. When a user revokes privacy consent, no standard runtime mechanism exists to propagate that change simultaneously and verifiably to all embedded SDKs, creating a race-condition window during which SDKs may continue collecting personal data. Furthermore, no existing system can produce cryptographic proof that a specific SDK binary version received and applied a specific consent state, leaving a critical gap in regulatory compliance demonstration. We present ConsentBus, a lightweight Swift package that addresses these technical deficiencies through: (1) a process-resident consent broker singleton executing all adapter dispatch on a dedicated serial context, eliminating propagation race conditions; (2) a normalized adapter protocol enabling purpose-granular dispatch across heterogeneous SDK consent APIs; (3) a receipt-chained tamper-evident audit ledger in which each entry incorporates HMAC-SHA256-hashed per-SDK propagation receipts; and (4) a Compliance Attestation Engine generating exportable, digitally-signed compliance artifacts with a three-way outcome classification (APPLIED \/ FAILED \/ NOT_SUPPORTED) and a coverage score computed over applicable SDKs only. We evaluate ConsentBus against five representative SDK adapters and demonstrate that the system eliminates consent propagation race conditions, produces tamper-evident compliance records verifiable without device access, and imposes negligible latency overhead on the consent propagation path.&nbsp;<\/jats:p>"},{"DOI":"10.5040\/9798216406884.ch-5","title":["Capturing Audit Trail Data"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2016]]},"container-title":["Building Trustworthy Digital Repositories"],"type":"other"},{"DOI":"10.1109\/bigdata66926.2025.11402054","title":["Cryptographic Provenance and AI-Generated Images"],"issued":{"date-parts":[[2025,12,8]]},"container-title":["2025 IEEE International Conference on Big Data (BigData)"],"type":"proceedings-article"}],"items-per-page":25,"query":{"start-index":0,"search-terms":null}}}
